En mai, nous avons rendu visite au Knafé: In May, we visited Knafé Stop, a Palestinian restaurant that serves authentic knafé from Nablus, a Palestinian city in the heart of the occupied West Bank. We spoke with the owner, Saad Antar, who left Nablus and settled in Montréal about 15 years ago to give his family and himself a better life.
Il s’agissait de notre première rencontr: It was our first time meeting an entrepreneur from the West Bank. We wanted to learn more about his experience, but above all about his life in his home country: what is life like under an apartheid regime? This curiosity came from the fact that the Palestinian perspective on this subject is almost never expressed in Canadian media.
Saad était très enthousiaste à l’idée de: Saad was very enthusiastic about sharing his experience with us. His attachment to his homeland was especially moving to witness during the interview. It shows that, despite the Israeli occupation’s attempts to erase Palestinian identity, the Palestinian people remain determined to preserve their culture.
Alors que les forces israéliennes intens: As Israeli forces intensify their violence against Palestinians in the West Bank and continue to deny them the right to life, we felt it was more important than ever to shine a light on Saad’s story and on the atrocities his people endure and that he has witnessed. It is a story marked by hardship, but also by his dedication to strengthening the presence of Palestinian heritage around the world.
<strong>À Laval, Saad Antar sert du <em>: In Laval, Saad Antar serves knafé while offering a glimpse of his hometown, Nablus, in Palestine. The city is in the occupied West Bank, and Saad shares his heritage with us while opening up about the brutal acts committed by the Israeli occupier against the Palestinian people. A portrait.
Son restaurant, le Knafé Stop, se trouve: His restaurant, Knafé Stop, is on boulevard des Laurentides and greets visitors with the sweet scent of pastry dough and syrup, mingled with the slightly salty smell of cheese.
L’intérieur est décoré de cartes géograp: The interior is decorated with maps of Palestine, framed artwork depicting the country, Palestinian flags and a panoramic reproduction of the Al-Aqsa Mosque, a sacred site in the occupied part of East Jerusalem.
Le plafond est couvert de keffiehs pales: The ceiling is covered with Palestinian keffiyehs, the traditional scarves with intricate patterns that have become a symbol of resistance.
Dans la salle principale, une télévision: In the main room, a television streams live, nonstop images of Nablus and its bustling streets. “At some point, you’ll be able to see the neighbourhood where I used to live,” he says.
La passion des habitants de Naplouse pou: Nablus residents’ passion for their culture allows them to show incredible resilience in the face of the occupation, a system that threatens their livelihoods every day. And that is reflected in Saad’s work.
Il se déplace avec aisance dans le resta: He moves easily around the restaurant, wears a radiant smile and greets people warmly. The subject of knafé lights up his eyes, and his hands come alive, conveying both his ambition and his devotion to his business. His tone turns affectionate when he speaks of his memories of Nablus, showing deep gratitude for his hometown.
<strong>Faire découvrir la ville de Napl: Introducing Montrealers to the city of Nablus
Saad a quitté Naplouse pour Montréal en: Saad left Nablus for Montréal in 2010, at the age of 19. His father had already been living in Montréal since 2000. They had to wait 10 years before he obtained permanent residence and could finally sponsor Saad and his brother.
Désireux de retrouver le goût du plat ty: Longing for the taste of his hometown’s signature dish, he set out to find a place in Montréal that made knafé. “We grew up in Nablus, so we have to eat [knafé] every day, maybe even twice a day,” he says with a laugh. The dessert is made of shredded pastry dough topped with cheese, soaked in syrup and sprinkled with crushed pistachios.
Cependant, Saad ne trouvait pas de <em>k: But Saad couldn’t find knafé that tasted like what he ate as a child. So he made it his mission to bring Nablus knafé to Montréal. In 2013, he went back to his hometown to find the recipe for this specialty. He ended up learning it at a pastry shop called Damascus’ Sweets. “In the history books, Nablus was called ‘Little Damascus,’” Saad explains enthusiastically.
Le premier restaurant de Saad était peti: Saad’s first restaurant was small, but it drew many customers. His first three years in business were marked by strong support from the Arab community, as well as a large clientele from around the world. “People encouraged me to open bigger places and more of them,” he says. Today, Knafé Stop has three locations, including one in downtown Montréal.
Après 15 ans au Québec, l’amour et l’att: After 15 years in Quebec, Saad’s love and attachment for his hometown have not faded. “Everything in Nablus is beautiful: its food, its streets, its people,” he says, pointing to the television screen and its images of lit-up streets as night falls over the city.
Considéré comme un dessert raffiné par t: Considered a refined dessert by all Palestinians, knafé holds special significance for the people of Nablus: the city is the birthplace of the dessert. “Palestinians from other cities used to come to Nablus to enjoy knafé, especially in the old city,” he explains.
Avec l’ouverture de Knafé Stop, Saad a n: With the opening of Knafé Stop, Saad has brought Montréal not only the sweet, original taste of knafé, but also a warm piece of his childhood. “I come from Nablus, so I know what it’s supposed to taste like. I serve something that is true to its roots,” he adds. The restaurant’s authenticity is also found in its use of ingredients imported from Palestine, such as the cheese and the melted butter. The coffee served there also comes from Palestine. “Sometimes people come just for the coffee.”
Knafé Stop propose aussi du Salam Cola c: Knafé Stop also offers Salam Cola as an alternative to Coca-Cola, in response to calls for a boycott in support of Palestine. “We boycott everything that supports or funds the occupation. Boycotting isn’t hard. Anyone who cares about this can find alternatives to what they need,” Saad says.
Saad retourne à Naplouse chaque année, p: Saad returns to Nablus every year, sometimes every five months. His journey to Palestine is long and full of obstacles. He begins by travelling to Jordan and crossing the land borders. Once in Palestine, he has to undergo questioning by Israeli authorities, then by Palestinian authorities, before he can head to his hometown.
Naplouse est une ville qui a beaucoup de: Nablus is a city with a lot of charm, but Israeli occupation forces have imposed conditions on the Palestinian population that make maintaining a decent life very difficult. There are checkpoints in every city in the West Bank, which makes travelling and accessing the region extremely complicated. “You can, for example, leave a place easily, but something can happen on the way back. They can close the checkpoint and you won’t be able to return,” he explains.
Sa dernière visite remonte au mois de ja: His last visit was this past January.
« Je suis resté deux mois à Naplouse. Je: “I stayed in Nablus for two months. I couldn’t leave, because the roads were very dangerous.”
Depuis qu’Israël a lancé son offensive d: Since Israel launched its bombing offensive on Gaza in October 2023, the restrictions imposed by the occupier in the West Bank have multiplied and tightened. According to Saad, Nablus is now surrounded by 12 electric gates that cannot be opened for Palestinians without the occupier’s permission.
Un miroir en forme de carte de la Palest: A mirror in the shape of a map of Palestine, with the names of the main cities. Photo credit: Sara Balkis
Selon le Bureau de la coordination des a: According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Israeli-imposed obstacles to movement in the West Bank rose from <l1>565</l1> to <l2>849</l2> between October 2023 and March 2025. They include permanent checkpoints, occasional checkpoints, roadblocks, earth mounds, road gates, earth walls and trenches.
Aux points de contrôle, le stress est im: At checkpoints, the stress is immense. How difficult the crossing is depends on the mood of the soldier on duty, Saad says. Many end up sleeping near checkpoints because they can’t get home. During Ramadan, the situation gets even worse. Waits grow longer, forcing people to break their fast and have their suhoor (the meal that breaks the day’s fast, Editor’s note) on the spot.
En outre, les forces d’occupation ont fa: In addition, the occupation forces have made raids a daily practice. “People are in the street, doing their shopping or going about their daily business when, suddenly, occupation soldiers burst in, block the exits, destroy property and assault them,” he reports. This violence tends to intensify and multiply during Ramadan.
« Et cela, c’est sans compter la violenc: “And that’s without counting settler violence, of course,” he adds. Palestinians, including children, are increasingly victims of attacks and intimidation by these Israeli settlers. “When you try to go to another city, at any moment you can run into settlers who try to attack you, either by throwing stones at your car or by surrounding you.”
Selon le ministère palestinien de la San: According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, <l1>more than 800 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by settlers and occupation forces since October 7, 2023</l1>.
L’aggravation du contrôle de l’occupatio: The tightening of the occupation’s control has had a negative effect on the economy, Saad notes, because the restrictions on people’s movement have made it almost impossible to take part in commercial activity.
Mais les difficultés rencontrées à Naplo: But the hardships in Nablus are not as severe as those faced by Palestinians in Gaza or in other West Bank cities, such as Jenin, Saad says. “That doesn’t mean there are no problems. There are many, but we say ‘Alhamdullilah’ (“praise be to God” in Arabic, Editor’s note); it’s not as bad as in other cities.”
L’occupation illégale de la Cisjordanie: Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank has lasted more than 50 years. “This is not a new phenomenon. We grew up facing these obstacles. It started even before we were born,” Saad points out. “But even in the face of this occupation, people do their best to make the most of the situation.”
« Ici, enchaîne-t-il, on peut se déplace: “Here,” he continues, “you can move around freely, no one violates your space. Your children can go to school and come back without the risk of someone getting in their way. That’s just how it is, unfortunately,” he says, with a hint of bitterness in his voice.
Néanmoins, il est convaincu qu’il retour: Still, he is convinced that he will one day go back to live in the West Bank. “I won’t stay here forever. I can’t leave my country. I can’t forget the place where I grew up, where my parents and my friends live. It’s impossible. But most of the time, I’ll be going back and forth between Canada and Palestine.”
